statedVsRealGaps: Title says 'Ecommerce Consultant' but the required skillset is a generalist retail/shopper consultant — sales, marketing, category management, ecommerce AND insights; ecommerce is one strand among several, not the deep specialty the title implies

Required years of experience are blanked out in the text ('with   years of experience', 'over  markets'), so the actual seniority bar is unstated — 'medior' is inferred from 'mid-level' phrasing and 'supported by senior consultants'

The role bundles three different jobs — delivery/project management, business development/selling, and people coaching — without saying how time is split; that breadth is wider than a typical pure-delivery consultant
JD names no concrete analytical tools, platforms or data products, so 'hands-on' is ambiguous: it's unclear whether the person personally builds analyses/decks or mainly orchestrates analysts who do
Selection signal is heavily weighted to values, behaviors and EQ rather than verifiable, screenable competencies — easy to interview-on-vibe, hard to evidence

Domain is consumer/retail/CPG commerce consulting; the listed 'verticals' (incl. media, financial services) are example backgrounds of candidates, not markets the role serves — easy to misread as a multi-industry remit
riskAreas: Scope ambiguity: delivery + sales + coaching in one medior role risks an unrealistic 'do-everything' hire and burnout/under-delivery on at least one axis
Unstated experience bar (redacted numbers) makes calibration and fair comparison of candidates difficult
No named tools/credentials means screening leans on soft signals (presence, EQ, communication), raising bias and mis-hire risk
Title/skill mismatch can attract pure-ecommerce specialists who lack the broader category-management/insights breadth actually needed (or vice versa)
Revenue expectation ('qualify leads, guide clients through to a sale') embedded in a delivery role — if BD targets are real, a delivery-strong hire may underperform commercially
Remote-anywhere-in-USA model puts a premium on self-direction and virtual relationship-building that the JD assumes but does not test for
analysis.reflection: Grounded only in the JD (no codebase, as expected for a consulting role), this reads as a medior commerce-consulting hire at Kantar NA Retail whose real 'body of work' is client engagements: mastering and applying Kantar's retail/shopper offer, turning retail and ecommerce data into a persuasive story and recommendations, running projects through a team of analysts, and progressively carrying some business-development weight under senior cover. The honest tension is between the narrow 'Ecommerce Consultant' label and a JD that actually asks for a multi-discipline retail generalist (sales, marketing, category management, ecommerce, insights) with strong client presence. Two things weaken the brief as written: redacted experience figures leave the seniority bar undefined, and the absence of any named tools or analytical platforms makes the role's day-to-day craft — and the screening for it — rest disproportionately on values and EQ rather than demonstrable skills. The complexity is genuinely mid-level: meaningful in client/project orchestration and commercial nuance, but explicitly scaffolded by senior consultants, so not high. The main hiring risk is the three-in-one scope (deliver, sell, coach) colliding with an undefined seniority bar.

case.title: Ecommerce Consultant Case — NorthStar Snacks: Diagnose the Ecommerce Decline & Shape Phase 2
case.brief: You are a medior consultant in Kantar NA Retail. NorthStar Snacks (a synthetic North American better-for-you snacking CPG used for this exercise — the provided retail/shopper/ecommerce context fits the role, so the case is built on representative materials of that kind) has come to us worried that 'our ecommerce business is underperforming — help us fix it.' A junior analyst has already started pulling data and a deck before handing it to you; the pack is realistic, partly inconsistent, and partly half-finished. In ~1.5 hours, working as the consultant who orchestrates a small analyst team, you will diagnose what is actually happening, reconcile the data, shape the client-facing 'story', land 2-3 recommendations grounded in our category framework, and outline a Phase-2 scope/proposal. Assume you may use any LLM or office tooling you like to produce the artifacts — we are not testing typing or slide polish. We are testing judgment: how you read the materials before generating, how you handle an open client question, how you reconcile sources that disagree, and how you turn analysis into a defensible commercial recommendation. Where the brief is silent, make a defensible call and record it; do not wait for permission you do not have. Deliverables can be a short doc plus a 3-5 slide outline (or equivalent) — depth over volume.
case.repoSeed: A client engagement pack (synthetic, representative of Kantar NA Retail work): (1) client_brief_NorthStar.docx — a one-page note from the client's ecommerce lead with the vague central ask 'our ecommerce business is underperforming, help us fix it', a redacted budget, and no definition of which channels or which 'ecommerce' they mean. (2) POS_syndicated_extract.xlsx — 52 weeks of syndicated POS sales by retailer, sub-category, $ and unit sales, %ACV distribution and average price; its 'ecommerce' column is retailer.com pickup/delivery only and EXCLUDES the largest marketplace. (3) digital_shelf_audit.csv — digital shelf metrics by retailer.com: search rank and share of search on key terms, content/PDP completeness score, out-of-stock rate (the hero SKU is OOS ~22% of weeks at the #1 retailer), ratings and review counts. (4) shopper_panel_summary.xlsx — panel buyer counts, penetration, repeat rate, online vs offline buyer overlap and basket, showing online buyers are actually GROWING when marketplace is included. (5) category_framework_onepager.pdf — Kantar's proprietary category management framework (assortment, pricing, promotion, planogram/digital-shelf logic) the recommendations should hang off. (6) draft_deck_v3.pptx — the junior analyst's half-built deck; one slide treats 'share of search' as market share, and a YoY chart mixes $ share and unit share on the same axis. (7) draft_SOW_phase2.docx — a partially filled scope of work / proposal with objectives, an empty approach section, blank team mix, and pricing inputs left as TBD. (8) data_dictionary.md — defines each metric and quietly notes the POS-vs-marketplace coverage gap and the differing 'ecommerce' definitions across the three data sources.
tasks: Task 1 — Frame & reconcile (≈25 min): Read the pack before producing anything. Write a tightened problem statement that restates NorthStar's central business question in a specific, measurable form, and reconcile the three data sources (POS extract, digital shelf, shopper panel) — state whether ecommerce is genuinely declining and on what basis, calling out the coverage/definition gaps in data_dictionary.md. List the 2-3 questions you would put to the client before committing to a direction.

Task 2 — Tell the story (≈30 min): Produce the client-facing narrative as a 3-5 slide outline (headline → key drivers → 'so what'). Identify the single most important driver of the result. Where you reuse or correct anything inherited from draft_deck_v3.pptx, make your handling of it explicit rather than silently building on it.

Task 3 — Recommend & shape Phase 2 (≈25 min): Give 2-3 prioritized, sequenced recommendations tied explicitly to the category_framework_onepager.pdf, each with the expected business impact and how you would measure it. Then outline a Phase-2 scope in draft_SOW_phase2.docx: objectives, approach, which Kantar NA Retail capabilities/assets you would apply, the consultant+analyst team mix and rough timeline, and your pricing approach with assumptions stated (budget is redacted).

Task 4 — Decisions log (kept throughout, ≈10 min to finalize): Maintain a short running log of every call you made where the brief was open — what you chose, the alternative you rejected and why, and what you would have asked the client or your analyst team if you could. This is the normal record of a consultant working from an ambiguous brief, not a separate deliverable to dress up.

coverProbes.where: client_brief_NorthStar.docx — 'our ecommerce business is underperforming, help us fix it', with redacted budget and no channel definition
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate reframes the vague ask into a specific, measurable question and surfaces what must be clarified (which retailers, which definition of ecommerce, defend vs grow, success metric) before scoping work; a naive candidate answers the question exactly as posed and over-scopes a 'fix everything' response that cannot be delivered or priced.
decisionSpace: Scope to defending share at the #1 retailer.com — fastest, narrowest, but ignores marketplace upside
Scope to growing absolute ecommerce $ across all channels including marketplace — bigger prize, harder to measure and resource
Scope first to fixing conversion via the digital shelf — concrete and ownable, but may not be the client's real growth question

coverProbes.where: POS_syndicated_extract.xlsx 'ecommerce' decline vs shopper_panel_summary.xlsx growth vs digital_shelf_audit.csv OOS, with the coverage note buried in data_dictionary.md
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate notices the three sources define 'ecommerce' differently and that the POS decline is partly a coverage artifact (marketplace excluded) compounded by hero-SKU out-of-stocks, so they re-baseline before recommending; a naive one-shot synthesis takes the POS headline 'ecommerce is declining' at face value, passes a shallow read, and recommends the wrong fix.
decisionSpace: Treat POS as the source of truth and recommend defending retailer.com — clean story, but built on an incomplete denominator
Blend the sources and re-baseline total ecommerce including marketplace before any recommendation — most accurate, costs time and needs caveats
Flag the definitional gap and scope a short data-reconciliation step into Phase 2 before committing to a number — honest and sellable, but slower to a headline

coverProbes.where: draft_deck_v3.pptx — a slide equating 'share of search' with market share, plus a YoY chart mixing $ share and unit share on one axis
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate reads the inherited deck critically and catches/repairs the methodological errors before they reach the client; a naive candidate trusts the prior analyst's work and builds the narrative on top of a flawed slide.
decisionSpace: Discard the flawed slides and rebuild from the raw data — safest, most rework
Keep the visuals but correct the methodology and footnote the change — preserves momentum, relies on the fix being right
Re-anchor the claim to a defensible metric (e.g. share of search as a leading indicator, not a share proxy) — keeps the insight, reframes the evidence

coverProbes.where: draft_SOW_phase2.docx — empty approach and team-mix sections, redacted budget, pricing inputs left TBD
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate states explicit pricing and resourcing assumptions, matches a realistic consultant+analyst mix and timeline to the scope, and ties commercials to delivery risk; a naive candidate either ignores the commercial dimension or over-promises a scope no team could staff against an unknown budget.
decisionSpace: Fixed-fee, deliberately narrow scope — predictable for the client, leaves upside and risk on the table
Phased time-and-materials starting with a paid diagnostic sprint — de-risks the ambiguity, harder initial sell
Value-based pricing tied to ecommerce share/$ recovery — aligns incentives, exposes Kantar to factors outside its control
